claims.text: Six hours of high-energy ball milling induces a critical level of lattice strain in equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling produces sufficient grain refinement to lower the activation-energy barrier for an FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C stabilizes the milling-induced metastable FCC-to-BCC transition.
SPS at 1000°C permits near-theoretical densification of ball-milled CoCrFeNiTi.
The 1000°C SPS window suppresses thermodynamically driven precipitation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern whether the processed alloy retains an FCC/BCC structure rather than forming a broader multiphase mixture.
Six-hour milling generates a high dislocation density and a nanocrystalline grain size below 20 nm.
Milling-induced defects and grain refinement alter local VEC and effective atomic-radius mismatch.
The milling-induced structural state shifts phase stability so that BCC is favored at lower temperatures than equilibrium predicts.
A VEC below approximately 8.0 is the critical threshold for BCC stability in CoCrFeNiTi.
Ti-induced lattice distortion and VEC reduction drive the FCC-to-BCC transition.
Rapid SPS heating and a 10-minute dwell at 1000°C kinetically trap a metastable FCC/BCC mixture.
The processed alloy will achieve greater than 98% of theoretical density.
The processed alloy will have a homogeneous nanocrystalline FCC/BCC dual-phase microstructure with no significant brittle Ti-rich HCP precipitates.
Grain-boundary strengthening will produce significantly higher Vickers hardness than in cast CoCrFeNiTi.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi typically has coarse dendritic microstructures, Ti-rich segregation, and lower hardness.
Sintering above 1050°C triggers excessive grain growth and precipitation of Ti-rich HCP phases.
The microstructural changes above 1050°C degrade mechanical properties and negate the benefits of milling.
Using a 100 gf Vickers load minimizes indentation-size effects and isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.
